title: Pink Cells, Red Jerseys, Blue Plates: Which Color Claims Are Real?
parts: A rainy street in Paris, painted in 1877. Now watch what happens when we change just one thing.
Red. Same street, same people. Does it still feel like the same afternoon?
Green. Yellow. Nothing moved. Only the color did.
Painters have always known this. Monet painted the same cathedral about thirty times, to catch how its color changed through the day.
And van Gogh wrote that he used red and green to express, in his words, the terrible passions of humanity.
So color really can change a scene. But then come the bigger promises: red makes you win, pink calms prisoners, blue kills your appetite.
We checked the studies behind the most repeated ones. The twist isn't that color does nothing. It's that it rarely does what the ads say.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Claim one: wearing red wins you fights.
A 2005 study of the Athens Olympics found red fighters won more — but only in close matches.
A bigger 2023 study, eight hundred seventy-eight taekwondo bouts, found something messier: in the old manual-scoring years, red helped men, but blue helped women in several brackets.
Once electronic scoring arrived, the effect disappeared.
A newer review found red winning fifty point five percent of the time — basically a coin flip.
Verdict: disputed, not a universal rule.
Claim two: red sharpens focus, blue sparks creativity.
A 2009 study in Science, over six hundred people, tested this directly.
Red backgrounds helped detail work, like proofreading. Blue backgrounds helped idea generation, like inventing new uses for an object.
That part is documented, straight from the study.
But skip any precise percentage you've seen online — that number traces back to a blog post, not the paper.
Claim three: a specific shade of pink, painted on prison cells, calms aggression.
The original 1979 report said so.
But the real controlled study — fifty-nine prisoners, pink cells against white cells — found zero measurable difference, at any point.
The "big percentage drop" some sources quote doesn't trace back to any real study. Verdict: myth.
Claim four: blue plates make you eat less.
A 2020 study, four hundred forty-eight people, tested color directly against appetite. No effect.
What does seem to matter is the contrast between food and plate, not the color itself — and even there, two studies contradict each other.
Verdict: myth on "blue kills appetite." Disputed on plate contrast.
Claim five: green relaxes you because it's the color of nature.
Looking at a green rooftop for forty seconds did improve attention in one study.
But no study has isolated the color green from simply looking at nature itself.
Verdict: disputed. It might be the scene, not the color.
Claim six: yellow raises anxiety, but also grabs attention better than blue.
The anxiety link comes from small, old, inconsistent studies — one even found the opposite.
The visibility claim is much stronger: Singapore's taxi fleet data found yellow taxis had about nine percent fewer accidents than blue ones, especially under street lighting.
Same color, two very different levels of evidence.
Verdict: disputed on anxiety, solid on visibility.
Claim seven, the one marketers repeat the most: color increases brand recognition by eighty percent.
We tried to find the original study behind that number.
We couldn't find it. No methodology, no year, no named researchers — just the same figure, copied page to page, even into patents.
Verdict: myth. Not disproven. Just never proven.
Notice the pattern.
Almost every viral color claim starts as a real, narrow study — and loses its nuance one retelling at a time.
By the time it reaches a caption or a slide, the sample size disappears, and the number gets rounder.
What survives the checking: color changes what you notice, and sometimes what you choose to look at.
What it mostly doesn't do, on this evidence, is flip a switch in how you feel.
So next time a color "fact" sounds too clean, ask which study it actually came from.
Symbols play the same trick. There's an eye on the dollar bill that people swear a secret society put there. We followed the paper trail. That's the next video.
